title: Explain the key components of a microservices architecture (API Gateway, Service Registry, Config Server, inter-service communication, DB-per-service, load balancer, monitoring/logging, circuit breaker).
shortTitle: Key components of a microservices architecture

s1_definition.profdef: A production microservices architecture is built from a standard set of components. The API Gateway is the single entry point handling routing, authentication, and rate limiting. The Service Registry (Eureka or Consul) lets services find each other by logical name instead of hardcoded IP. The Config Server centralizes externalized configuration so services read settings from one place. Inter-service communication is synchronous (REST, Feign, gRPC) or asynchronous (Kafka, RabbitMQ). Database-per-service gives each service a private store. A client-side or server-side load balancer spreads traffic across instances. Monitoring and logging (Prometheus, Grafana, ELK, Zipkin) provide observability. A circuit breaker (Resilience4j) stops cascading failures.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a large campus. The API Gateway is the main reception that checks your ID and directs you. The Service Registry is the campus directory that tells reception which building the Payment department is in today, because departments move. The Config Server is the central rulebook every department reads from. The load balancer is the queue manager sending you to whichever teller counter is free. Monitoring is the CCTV and alarm room. The circuit breaker is the "counter temporarily closed" sign so customers do not pile up at a desk that cannot help them.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A production microservices architecture is built from a standard set of components. The API Gateway is the single entry point handling routing, authentication, and rate limiting. The Service Registry (Eureka or Consul) lets services find each other by logical name instead of hardcoded IP. The Config Server centralizes externalized configuration so services read settings from one place. Inter-service communication is synchronous (REST, Feign, gRPC) or asynchronous (Kafka, RabbitMQ). Database-per-service gives each service a private store. A client-side or server-side load balancer spreads traffic across instances. Monitoring and logging (Prometheus, Grafana, ELK, Zipkin) provide observability. A circuit breaker (Resilience4j) stops cascading failures.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India as a large campus. The API Gateway is the main reception that checks your ID and directs you. The Service Registry is the campus directory that tells reception which building the Payment department is in today, because departments move. The Config Server is the central rulebook every department reads from. The load balancer is the queue manager sending you to whichever teller counter is free. Monitoring is the CCTV and alarm room. The circuit breaker is the "counter temporarily closed" sign so customers do not pile up at a desk that cannot help them.

**One line to remember:** Gateway is the front door, Registry is the directory, Config Server is the rulebook, load balancer spreads traffic, each service owns its DB, Kafka and REST connect them, and monitoring plus circuit breakers keep it alive.

sections.s2_technical:
The API Gateway is the single public entry point. In Spring Cloud Gateway a route is a predicate plus filters, for example routing `Path=/api/v1/payments/**` to `lb://payment-service` with `CircuitBreaker` and `RequestRateLimiter` filters. The `lb://` prefix means "load-balanced lookup through the registry". This keeps authentication, rate limiting, and cross-cutting concerns in one place instead of duplicated in every service.

The Service Registry solves the problem that service instances come and go with scaling and deploys, so you cannot hardcode addresses. Each service registers itself on startup, for example with `@EnableEurekaClient`, and callers resolve the logical name. The Config Server externalizes configuration: a service reads `spring.config.import=configserver:` and pulls its `application.yml` from a central Git-backed server, so you change a timeout once without rebuilding.

Inter-service communication has two flavors. Synchronous uses a declarative client like `@FeignClient(name="account-service")` with a method `void debit(@PathVariable String id, @RequestBody DebitRequest r)`, where Feign plus the registry plus a client-side load balancer picks a healthy instance. Asynchronous uses `kafkaTemplate.send("payment-events", paymentId, event)` so the Notification Service reacts later without the Payment Service waiting. Database-per-service means the Payment Service keeps its payments table private; other services get data by calling it or by consuming its events into a local read model.

Resilience and observability bind it together. A circuit breaker `@CircuitBreaker(name="accountService", fallbackMethod="debitFallback")` moves CLOSED to OPEN after a failure-rate threshold and fails fast, then HALF_OPEN tests recovery; you pair it with a timeout and a bulkhead. Monitoring uses Prometheus to scrape metrics and Grafana to dashboard them, ELK for structured logs, and Zipkin with a shared traceId for distributed traces. The senior-level nuance is that these components are not optional extras: without a registry you get brittle addresses, without a config server you get config drift, and without circuit breakers one slow dependency takes the whole system down.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the Payment Service must call the Account Service to debit Rajesh. Problem 1 — the Account Service runs three instances that scale up and down, so hardcoding one IP breaks the moment that instance dies. This is exactly what the Service Registry plus load balancer solve: the caller asks for the logical name "account-service" and gets a healthy instance. Problem 2 — the debit timeout is set in ten different services and someone needs to change it bank-wide. This is exactly what the Config Server solves: change it once, every service picks it up. Problem 3 — when the Account Service is slow the Payment Service must not hang forever. This is exactly what the circuit breaker solves.

The mini-project builds a tiny `ServiceRegistry`, a `LoadBalancer` that round-robins across registered instances, an `AccountClient` that resolves "account-service" through the registry and calls a healthy instance with a circuit breaker, and a `ConfigServer` that supplies the debit timeout. A runnable demo registers three Account Service instances, performs several debits, and shows traffic spreading across instances and failing over when one instance is down.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four debit requests of 50,000 rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001), across three Account Service instances.

Step 1: Three Account Service instances register themselves in the Service Registry under the logical name "account-service". The data here is the list of addresses the registry holds.

Step 2: The Payment Service's `AccountClient` wants to debit Rajesh. It asks the `LoadBalancer` to choose an instance. The load balancer asks the registry for healthy instances and round-robins, so the first call goes to 10.0.0.1, the next to 10.0.0.2, the next to 10.0.0.3, then back to 10.0.0.1.

Step 3: Before calling, the client reads `account.debit.timeout-ms` from the Config Server, getting 2000. This value is centralized, so changing it does not require touching the client code.

Step 4: Instance 10.0.0.3 goes down and is marked unhealthy. The registry now returns only two healthy instances, so the load balancer spreads traffic only across 10.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.2. No request is sent to the dead instance.

Step 5: In real Spring code each of these debits would be wrapped in a circuit breaker, so if the chosen instance kept failing, the breaker would open and the client would fail fast with a fallback instead of hanging.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A microservices architecture is assembled from a standard set of components, and in interviews I describe each by the problem it solves. The API Gateway is the single public entry point that handles routing, authentication, and rate limiting, so these cross-cutting concerns live in one place instead of being copied into every service. The Service Registry, usually Eureka or Consul, solves the problem that instances come and go with scaling and deploys: services register under a logical name and callers resolve that name instead of hardcoding an address.

The Config Server centralizes externalized configuration, so when I need to change a timeout bank-wide at National Bank of India I change it once and every service picks it up without a rebuild. Inter-service communication comes in two flavors: synchronous with REST, Feign, or gRPC when the caller needs an answer immediately, and asynchronous with Kafka or RabbitMQ when the caller should not wait. Database-per-service keeps each service's data private, so the Payment Service never reaches into the Account Service's tables; it calls the service or consumes its events.

A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy instances, and in Spring Cloud this is client-side through the registry. Resilience comes from circuit breakers in Resilience4j, which move from closed to open after a failure-rate threshold and fail fast so one slow dependency does not take the whole system down, paired with timeouts and bulkheads.

Finally, observability ties everything together: Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, the ELK stack for structured logs, and Zipkin with a shared traceId so I can follow one of Rajesh's transfers across the gateway, payment, and account services. The point I always make to an interviewer is that none of these are optional luxuries. Without a registry you get brittle addresses, without a config server you get config drift, and without circuit breakers one failing dependency cascades into a full outage.
